Okay, so I'm trying to figure out which substance, when mixed with water, produces the best conductor of electricity. The options are table salt, granulated sugar, carbon dioxide, and motor oil. I remember from school that conductors are materials that allow electricity to flow through them easily. I think it has something to do with ions in the solution.

First, I'll go through each option one by one. Table salt is sodium chloride, right? When it dissolves in water, it breaks down into sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl−) ions. Those ions are charged, so they can move freely when an electric current is applied, which makes the solution conduct electricity well. That makes sense because I've heard that saltwater is a good conductor.

Next, granulated sugar is sucrose. I think sugar doesn't dissolve into ions. It's a non-electrolyte, so when you mix it with water, it just stays as molecules without breaking apart. Without free ions, the solution can't conduct electricity as well. I remember a science fair project where they compared saltwater and sugarwater, and the saltwater conducted electricity better. So sugar probably isn't the best conductor.

Carbon dioxide is a gas, and when it dissolves in water, it forms carbonic acid. I think that doesn't release many ions. Maybe a little, but not nearly as much as table salt. So the solution wouldn't conduct electricity very well.

Motor oil is nonpolar, and water is polar. They don't mix well, so motor oil stays separate. Without being dissolved, it can't carry charges, so it doesn't conduct electricity at all. That's why I've heard that oil and water don't mix and don't conduct electricity.

Putting it all together, table salt provides the most ions, making the solution a strong conductor. The other options either don't provide ions or don't provide enough. So the best conductor should be table salt.
</think>
